segments.say: Lesson 16. Design a Rate Limiter. Token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed and sliding windows, and distributed limiting with Redis.

A rate limiter caps how many requests a user or client can make in a time window (for example 100 per minute) to protect the system from abuse and overload. Here is an analogy. A nightclub bouncer with a clicker: only so many people in per minute; the rest wait outside.

Why does this matter? Common standalone question and a building block of every public A P I. A few key words. Token bucket: Tokens refill steadily; each request spends one. Sliding window: Count requests in the last N seconds. 429: "Too Many Requests" status code. Fail-open / closed: Allow / block traffic if the limiter itself fails.
Token bucket (capacity 4, refill 1/sec). Each user (or A P I key) has a bucket that holds up to 4 tokens and refills at 1 token/sec.
A burst of 3 requests: each takes a token leads to allowed. Bursts up to capacity are fine.
Next request takes the last token. The one after finds the bucket empty leads to H T T P 429 with a Retry-After header.
Refill is computed lazily: tokens equals min(cap, tokens plus elapsed times rate). Store just (tokens, last refill ts) per key.
Alternative: sliding window, which counts requests in the last 60 s. Precise, but the log costs memory. A sliding window counter approximates it cheaply.
Distributed rate limiting. Enforce limits at the edge (A P I gateway or middleware) before requests consume backend resources.
Many gateway instances must share counters, so keep them in Redis. Use an atomic Lua script (or I N C R plus EXPIRE) so check-and-decrement can't race.
Rules per user tier, endpoint and I P live in config and are cached locally in the gateway.
Allowed leads to forward. Denied, giving 429 plus X-RateLimit-Remaining headers. If Redis is down, decide fail-open (availability) or fail-closed (protection).

Requirements to clarify. Limit by what? User I D, A P I key, I P, endpoint. Hard or soft limits? Bursts allowed. Distributed across many servers or regions? Latency budget (must add <1–2 ms). Behaviour on limiter failure: fail open or fail closed.

Scaling details. Shard Redis by key. Local in-memory pre-checks for very hot keys. Multi-region: per-region limits or async global sync (approximate is usually fine). Return standard headers so clients can back off politely.

Say it in the interview. "I'd use a token bucket per A P I key since it allows controlled bursts, stored as (tokens, last refill) in Redis and updated atomically via Lua at the A P I gateway. Rules are per tier and endpoint. Responses carry 429 with Retry-After and rate-limit headers, and if Redis fails I'd fail open for normal endpoints but fail closed for expensive or abuse-prone ones.".

Let's compare. Token bucket: up to capacity, tiny (2 values), good, most popular (A W S, Stripe). Leaky bucket: smooths to constant rate, queue, good, traffic shaping. Fixed window counter: 2 times burst at window edges, tiny, edge spikes, simplest. Sliding window log:, high (timestamps), exact, costly at scale. Sliding window counter:, tiny, approximate, good, great trade-off.

A likely interview question: Design a distributed rate limiter. A strong answer: Token bucket per key in Redis (tokens, timestamp), atomic Lua updates at the gateway, config-driven rules per tier and endpoint, 429 plus headers, local caching for hot keys, an explicit fail-open/closed policy, and monitoring of rejections.
That's it for Design a Rate Limiter. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
